note: PGL.IP.API is IP's .NET/COM AUTOMATION + DATA-ACCESS API (curves, curve-sets, wells, zones, parameters, units, statistics, plots, reporting). It is NOT a petrophysical-equation library: no Archie/Vsh/porosity/Sw math functions are exposed here. FE math lives in compiled modules (UserProgram.dll) and is reached from user code via the Formula language and the UserProgram/ip2py on-ramps. Contrast Techlog, whose Python API (TechlogQuanti) DOES expose equation-level FE functions.

types.summary: Represents the mode of a T:PGL.IP.API.ICurveDataIterator.

members.summary: Enumerator is in a Normal mode, using a Curve Set Depth Curve as the reference Curve. When enumerating, the next depth value will be the next value in the depth reference Curve, top down. Curve data can be read and updated. The depths returned by the enumerator will always be depths present in the depth reference Curve.

Enumerator is using a non standard Depth Curve as the reference Curve, where data is being enumerated at a fixed step. When enumerating, the next depth value will be the current value + the fixed step. Curve data can only be read in this mode. The depths returned by the enumerator may not always be depths present in the depth reference Curve.

Enumerator is in an Array Reference mode, using a Curve with a Y dimension as the reference Curve. When enumerating, the Y dimension of the reference Curve will be enumerated (1 to length) before being reset, then moving to the next depth value in the depth reference Curve, top down, and repeating. Curve data can be read and updated. The depths returned by the enumerator will be interpolated between depth values in the depth reference Curve, based on the proportion through the Y dimension.

members.summary: Single precision data, 32-bit (4-byte). Single variables are stored as signed IEEE 32-bit (4-byte) single-precision floating-point numbers ranging in value from -3.4028235E+38 through -1.401298E-45 for negative values and from 1.401298E-45 through 3.4028235E+38 for positive values. Single-precision numbers store an approximation of a real number.

Double precision data, 64-bit (8-byte). Double variables are stored as signed IEEE 64-bit (8-byte) double-precision floating-point numbers ranging in value from -1.79769313486231570E+308 through -4.94065645841246544E-324 for negative values and from 4.94065645841246544E-324 through 1.79769313486231570E+308 for positive values.

Variable length strings. Null values are discarded and stored as empty strings instead. String variables are stored as sequences of unsigned 16-bit (2-byte) numbers ranging in value from 0 through 65535. Each number represents a single Unicode character. A string can contain up to approximately 2 billion (2 ^ 31) Unicode characters.
Short precision data, 16-bit (2-byte). Short variables are stored as signed 16-bit (2-byte) integers with values ranging from -32768 through +32767.
Unsigned Short precision data, 16-bit (2-byte). Short variables are stored as unsigned 16-bit (2-byte) integers with values ranging from 0 through +65535.
Byte data, 8-bit (1-byte). Byte variables are stored as unsigned 8-bit (1-byte) integers with values ranging from 0 through 255.
Signed byte data, 8-bit (1-byte). Byte variables are stored as signed 8-bit (1-byte) integers with values ranging from -128 to 127.

Half precision data (binary16), 16-bit (2-byte). Half variables are stored as signed IEEE 754-2008 16-bit (2-byte) half-precision floating-point numbers (officially referred to as binary 16), with values ranging from -65504 to 65504.
